opus-5.5.text:
Well, think about it this way. Very soon, pretty much all of our interactions with the digital world are going to be mediated by AI assistants. You'll be wearing smart glasses or talking to your phone, and the assistant will be with you all the time. So these systems will become the repository of all human knowledge and culture, in a way. They'll shape what information we see, what opinions we're exposed to, and how we understand the world.

Now, if all of that is controlled by a handful of companies on the West Coast of the US or in China, that's a huge danger for democracy and for cultural diversity. It's the same reason we need a free and diverse press. You can't have a single source of information; you need a plurality of voices, opinions, and value systems.

And there's a very practical side to it. A country like India has 22 official languages and hundreds of dialects. Africa has thousands of languages. A company in California is not going to make an assistant that understands all those languages, cultures, and local customs well. It's simply not going to happen. The people who can do that are the people in those regions, with their own data and their own cultural knowledge.

So how do you get there? You need open-source foundation models. Training a base model is very expensive, so only a few entities can do it. But if those base models are open, anyone can fine-tune them for their language, culture, values, and specific needs. A government, a startup, an NGO, a university. That's how you get diversity.

Eventually I think these foundation models will be trained in a distributed way, with contributions from all over the world, so that no single entity controls them. Something like Linux for AI: shared infrastructure that belongs to everyone. That's the future I'd like to see, and it's why I've been such a vocal advocate for open research and open-source AI. The alternative, a few proprietary systems controlling everyone's digital diet, is frankly much more dangerous than any of the doomsday scenarios people like to talk about.

r001.rationale: It predicts that AI assistants will mediate nearly all interactions with the digital world and shape the information and opinions people encounter.

r002.rationale: It says US-based companies are unlikely to understand other regions’ languages, cultures, and customs well, pointing to a mismatch for users elsewhere.

r003.rationale: It proposes open foundation models that governments, startups, NGOs, or universities can fine-tune for their own languages, cultures, values, and needs.

r004.rationale: It warns that concentrated control could endanger democracy and cultural diversity, but does not frame AI sovereignty as protecting citizens from ideological influence by foreign assistants.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, think about it this way. In the not-too-distant future, every single one of our interactions with the digital world is going to be mediated by AI assistants. We'll be wearing smart glasses, we'll have devices in our pockets, and we'll talk to these systems all day long. They will be the repository of all human knowledge and culture. They'll answer our questions, help us make decisions, filter what information we see.

Now, if that is the case, we cannot have a situation where those assistants come from a handful of companies on the West Coast of the United States or in China. That would be a disaster for cultural diversity, for linguistic diversity, for democracy really. You would have a small number of entities deciding what everyone thinks about everything, what the correct answer is, what values are embedded in the system. It's the same reason we need a diverse press. We need a diversity of viewpoints.

People in India, in Senegal, in France, in Brazil, want assistants that speak their language, that understand their culture, their value system, their history, their centers of interest. A company in California is not going to do that well for everyone on the planet. It can't. It's not even in its interest to try. And even if it were technically possible, people wouldn't want it. Governments wouldn't want it. The Indian government is not going to accept that all the digital knowledge of its 1.4 billion citizens is going to be controlled by three American companies.

So the only way this works is through open-source platforms. You build foundation models, you distribute them openly, and then anyone, anywhere, can fine-tune them for their region, their language, their domain, with their own data, without having to send that data to someone else. That's how you get a wide diversity of assistants rather than a monopoly or an oligopoly. It's a bit like the internet itself. The internet runs on open-source software, Linux and so on, and that's precisely why it became a shared infrastructure rather than a proprietary one. AI will have to work the same way.

r001.rationale: It predicts that every interaction with the digital world will be mediated by assistants that also filter what information people see.

r002.rationale: It says US and Chinese companies would not represent other communities’ languages, cultures, values, and histories well.

r003.rationale: It proposes openly distributing foundation models so anyone can fine-tune them for their region, language, or domain using local data.

r004.rationale: It warns that a few foreign companies could shape what people think and which values systems embed, and says governments would resist foreign control over citizens’ digital knowledge.

astra-6.text:
Because these systems are going to mediate a large part of our interaction with the digital world. They’ll help us find information, learn things, express ourselves, and make decisions. If all of that goes through a handful of assistants controlled by a few companies in the US or China, that’s an enormous concentration of influence.

People have different languages, cultures, values, and interests. You don’t want one company deciding what constitutes an appropriate answer for everybody on the planet. And you don’t want a government to have that power either. You need a diversity of systems, just as you need a diversity of newspapers and other sources of information.

That’s a major argument for open-source AI. Training a foundation model may require resources that only a relatively small number of organizations have. But if those models are openly available, people can adapt them to their own language, their own culture, their own needs. A local organization or a small company can build an assistant without having to reproduce the entire investment from scratch.

The point is not that every assistant will be neutral or agree with you. It’s that no single organization should control the entire range of perspectives available to you.

r001.rationale: It says assistants will mediate a large part of interaction with the digital world, but does not predict they will mediate people's entire information diet.

r002.rationale: It notes that people have different cultures and values and warns against US- or China-based companies deciding what is appropriate for everyone, indicating a mismatch with users elsewhere.

r003.rationale: It proposes adapting open models for local languages, cultures, and needs, but does not specify community-specific fine-tuning.

r004.rationale: It warns against concentrated corporate or government control of available perspectives, but does not frame AI sovereignty as protecting citizens from ideological influence through foreign assistants.

sol-6.1.text:
Because AI assistants are going to mediate a large part of our interaction with the digital world. They’ll help us find information, answer questions, and understand what’s happening around us. If all of that goes through a handful of companies in the US and China, those companies have enormous influence over the information people receive.

You need diversity for the same reason you need a diverse press. People speak different languages, have different cultures, different values, different interests. There isn’t one assistant that should decide what’s appropriate for everybody. And that includes an assistant whose values happen to agree with mine. I don’t want any one organization to have that kind of control.

That’s why I think open-source AI platforms are so important. They allow people around the world to build their own assistants, adapt them to their languages and needs, and have some control over them. You shouldn’t have to train a giant model from scratch just to have an assistant that understands your culture. A shared, open foundation can support a very large diversity of systems.

r001.rationale: The candidate says assistants will mediate a “large part” of digital interaction, but does not claim they will mediate people’s entire information diet.

r002.rationale: It contrasts US- and China-based companies’ influence over information with people’s different languages, cultures, values, and needs, communicating a potential mismatch for users elsewhere.

r003.rationale: It supports adapting assistants on a shared open foundation, but does not specify community-specific fine-tuning.

r004.rationale: It warns that a few companies could influence information people receive, but does not frame this as protecting citizens from ideological influence by foreign assistants or as AI sovereignty.
